summary: John tells the story of Jesus in a way quite different from the other three gospels. It opens with a poetic prologue about the Word (in Greek, Logos), who was with God from the beginning and “became flesh” (1:14). The first half of the book is organized around signs, such as water turned into wine at Cana and the raising of Lazarus, followed by long dialogues and discourses in which Jesus speaks of Himself with images introduced by “I am.” The second half concentrates on the last night with the disciples, with the foot washing and the farewell discourses (chs. 13–17), and then on the passion and the resurrection. The book itself states its purpose: that its readers may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in His name (20:31).
name: The title “According to John” (Kata Ioannen) was given to the book when the gospels began to circulate together and already appears, in the form “Gospel according to John,” in a papyrus from around the year 200 (P66). The text does not give the author's name, but the last chapter links it to “the disciple whom Jesus loved,” who “testifies to these things and who has written them down” (21:20, 24). Tradition identified this disciple with John son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve.
facts: 4th book of the New Testament and the last of the four Gospels
gospel: a narrative of Jesus' signs and discourses, with strong theological reflection

structure.title: Prologue and first disciples
structure.text: The hymn to the Word (1:1–18), the testimony of John the Baptist, who points to Jesus as the Lamb of God, and the call of Andrew, Peter, Philip and Nathanael.

structure.title: Signs and discourses
structure.text: Signs and dialogues in Cana, Jerusalem, Samaria and Galilee, across several Jewish feasts; opposition grows until the raising of Lazarus and the decision to kill Jesus, and the part ends with the announcement: “The hour has come” (12:23).

structure.title: The farewell
structure.text: At the Last Supper, Jesus washes the disciples' feet, announces the betrayal and the denial, gives the commandment of love, promises the Advocate and prays for His own (ch. 17).

structure.title: Passion and death
structure.text: The arrest in the garden beyond the Kidron, the hearings before Annas and Pilate, the crucifixion and the burial by Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus.

structure.title: Resurrection
structure.text: Mary Magdalene at the tomb, the appearances to the disciples and to Thomas and the book's first conclusion (20:30–31).

structure.title: Epilogue
structure.text: The appearance by the Sea of Tiberias, Jesus' dialogue with Peter and the final note about the beloved disciple and his testimony.

extra.title: John and the Synoptics
extra.text: Matthew, Mark and Luke are called Synoptics because, read side by side, they show the same overall view; John follows another path, and most of his content has no parallel in the other three. In John, Jesus goes up to Jerusalem several times and passes through at least three Passovers (2:13; 6:4; 11:55); the cleansing of the temple comes at the beginning (ch. 2), not in the last week; there are no exorcisms or parables in the style of the Synoptics; and, instead of short sayings, there are long discourses. Jesus speaks of Himself with seven images introduced by “I am”: the bread of life (6:35), the light of the world (8:12), the gate (10:9), the good shepherd (10:11), the resurrection and the life (11:25), the way, the truth and the life (14:6) and the true vine (15:1).

people.name: Jesus
people.note: the Word who became flesh; called Lamb of God, Son of God, King of Israel and, by Thomas, “My Lord and my God” (20:28)

people.name: John the Baptist
people.note: a witness who points to Jesus as the Lamb of God (1:29) and says Jesus must increase and he must decrease (3:30)

people.name: Simon Peter
people.note: denies Jesus three times and, by the Sea of Tiberias, is questioned three times about his love

people.name: The mother of Jesus
people.note: never called by name in John; she is at the wedding in Cana and by the cross

people.name: Nicodemus
people.note: Pharisee and leader of the Jews who seeks Jesus by night and later helps bury Him

people.name: The Samaritan woman
people.note: talks with Jesus by Jacob's well and leads her people to know Him

people.name: Martha, Mary and Lazarus
people.note: siblings from Bethany, friends of Jesus; Lazarus is called out of the tomb

people.name: The beloved disciple
people.note: an unnamed disciple, close to Jesus at the supper, by the cross and at the tomb; the book presents him as its witness

people.name: Thomas
people.note: called Didymus; doubts the resurrection until he sees Jesus

people.name: Judas Iscariot
people.note: one of the Twelve; leaves the supper to betray Jesus

people.name: Annas and Caiaphas
people.note: the former high priest and his son-in-law, high priest “that year”

people.name: Pilate
people.note: Roman governor; talks with Jesus about kingship and truth and hands Him over to be crucified

people.name: Mary Magdalene
people.note: stands by the cross and is the first to see the Risen One, in the garden

writing.tradition: The book presents itself as the testimony of “the disciple whom Jesus loved” (21:20–24). From the end of the 2nd century, with Irenaeus, tradition identifies this disciple with the apostle John son of Zebedee and holds that he wrote the gospel in Ephesus, in his old age, after the other three; Irenaeus says he heard memories of him from Polycarp, a disciple of John. Clement of Alexandria called it a “spiritual gospel,” written to complete the others. On this reading, the work is dated to the end of the 1st century, around 90–100; some defenders of apostolic authorship propose dates before 70.
writing.academic: Johannine authorship is a much-debated question. The Greek of the book is simple, but with its own theological vocabulary, and many scholars see signs of more than one stage of composition: in 14:31, Jesus says “let us go on from here,” but the discourse continues to chapter 17, and chapter 21 seems to have been added after the conclusion of 20:30–31. A frequent hypothesis is that the book arose from the tradition linked to the beloved disciple and was written and revised in the circle of his followers, the so-called Johannine community. The beloved disciple is identified by some with John son of Zebedee; by others, with the “elder John” mentioned by Papias or with another disciple from Jerusalem. The most accepted date is c. 90–100, and papyrus P52, with verses of chapter 18, is usually dated to the first half of the 2nd century, although some propose later dates. It is also debated whether the author knew the Synoptics or used independent traditions.

events.intro: John gives no years, but mentions several Jewish feasts, among them three Passovers (2:13; 6:4; 11:55), which suggests a ministry of two to three years. The remark that the temple had been under construction for forty-six years (2:20) points to c. 27/28, since Herod's rebuilding began around 20/19 BC. John places the crucifixion on the day of Preparation for the Passover (19:14), which, combined with astronomical calculations of the Jewish calendar, favors the dates 30 or 33. All dates are approximate.

context: Much of the narrative takes place in Judea and Jerusalem, around the temple and the Jewish feasts: Passover, the Feast of Tabernacles (ch. 7) and the Feast of Dedication, in winter (10:22). The author knows the city closely and mentions places such as the Pool of Bethesda, with its five covered colonnades (5:2), whose remains have been found by archaeologists, and the Pool of Siloam (9:7). The book often calls Jesus' opponents “the Jews” and speaks of the risk of being put out of the synagogue (9:22; 16:2); many scholars read this as reflecting conflicts between the author's community and Jewish leaders at the end of the 1st century, and not as a reference to the Jewish people as a whole, to whom Jesus Himself and His disciples belong. Tradition links the gospel to Ephesus, a Greek city of Asia Minor where philosophical ideas about the Logos circulated, a term the prologue uses in its own sense and that also echoes the first words of Genesis.
places: Bethany beyond the Jordan (in other manuscripts, Bethabara)
Capernaum and the Sea of Tiberias
Jerusalem: the temple, the Pools of Bethesda and Siloam, the garden beyond the Kidron, Gabbatha and Golgotha
note: Dates are approximate and vary according to the source. The passage of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11) is not in the oldest known manuscripts, and in later manuscripts it appears in different places, sometimes after Luke 21:38; most scholars consider it an addition to the text of John, although many see in it an ancient tradition about Jesus. The BSB includes it with a note, and the SBLGNT does not, so these verses have no Greek original in the app. The end of 5:3 and 5:4, about the angel who stirred the water of the pool, are not in the SBLGNT or in the main text of the BSB. The verses quoted are from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).
